passage:
At the temple fair in Kodur, Pranav lost the slow-cycle race to Ganga for the second year. That evening he wheeled his cycle to the dry canal bank and practised balancing, feet up, counting under his breath. 'If I practise every day, next year I'll win,' he told his grandmother.
He practised all month. On race day he was steady and slow, ahead of everyone, until his old chain snapped and he tipped into the dust.
He sat there, face hot. 'I should have practised more.'
Ganga dropped her own cycle and crouched beside him. 'You were winning. The chain broke. That's not your legs.'
Pranav looked at the chain lying in two pieces. Slowly, he nodded. 'Next year I'll practise. And oil the chain.'

qa.q: What did Pranav do at the dry canal bank?
qa.a: He practised balancing on his cycle, feet up, counting under his breath.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the chain snapped, and why did he blame his practice?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and blamed himself, believing his effort decides the result, even though the broken chain was not in his control.

qa.q: What turning point helped Pranav see the loss more fairly?
qa.a: Ganga pointed out that he was winning and the chain broke, not his legs; then Pranav chose to keep practising and also oil the chain.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Pranav's month of practice?
qa.a: Ganga probably respects it, since she watched him lead the race, and she wants him to know the fall was not his fault.

grounding: Shows a child who believes practice shapes results and tries again after losing, and who briefly blames himself for something outside his control.

passage:
Priscila lost to Jamal in four moves on Tuesday, a trap she had never seen. She didn't cry. She asked him to show it to her again, then set it up on her kitchen table in Porto that night, playing both sides while her dad washed the dishes.
'Luck,' her brother said.
'No. I didn't know the trap. Now I do.'
By Friday she had beaten the trap twice in practice. In the real rematch, though, the school bell rang mid-game and the teacher called a draw, and Priscila stomped home saying she should have played faster.
Her dad dried his hands. 'Could you have made the bell ring later?'
She thought about that. 'No,' she admitted. 'But I can practise the trap more.'

qa.q: Where did Priscila set up the trap to practise it?
qa.a: On her kitchen table in Porto, playing both sides.

qa.q: Why did Priscila tell her brother 'No' when he said it was luck?
qa.a: She believed she lost because she didn't know the trap yet, which is something she could learn, not luck.

qa.q: What choice did Priscila make after her dad's question about the bell?
qa.a: She admitted the bell was not in her control and chose to keep practising the trap instead of blaming herself for the draw.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel when Priscila asked him to show the trap again?
qa.a: Jamal might be surprised or pleased that she wanted to learn from losing, and could start to see her as a serious rival.

grounding: Shows a child who treats a loss as something to learn from and practises, while an adult helps her not blame herself for what she could not control.

passage: Vinita came fourth in the colony skipping race, and instead of sulking she went straight to the terrace with her rope. "If I practise double jumps every evening, I'll get faster," she told her friend Nikita, and counted aloud till dark. Two weeks later she came second. But on the day of the inter-colony final it poured, and the event was cancelled. Vinita sat on the stairs, arms round her knees. "I should have practised more. Then maybe..." Nikita frowned. "Maybe what? Make it stop raining?" Vinita opened her mouth, then shut it. After a moment she laughed, wiping her eyes. "Okay. That one's not my fault."

qa.q: Where did Vinita practise?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling on the stairs after the final was cancelled?
qa.a: She was disappointed and blaming herself, as if more practice could have changed the rain.

qa.q: What helped Vinita see the situation more clearly?
qa.a: Nikita's question about the rain, which showed some things are beyond her control.

qa.q: How might Nikita feel watching Vinita blame herself for the rain?
qa.a: Nikita seems puzzled and a little amused, wanting to help her friend see sense.

grounding: Shows a child who believes practice shapes results, tries again after losing, and briefly blames herself for something beyond control.

passage:
"Mummy, I lost the quiz because I didn't read the science chapter properly. Next time I'm making flashcards."
"That's a good plan, Trisha."
"And I'll ask Ma'am for old papers. I can do better."
Ritu smiled. "You really believe that, don't you?"
"Of course. If I work, it changes." Trisha stopped. "Mummy, is Nani sick because I didn't visit on Sunday?"
Ritu put down the dishcloth. "No, beta. Nani is sick because she's old and her lungs are weak. Nothing you did caused it."
"But if I'd gone..."
"You'd have given her a hug. That's lovely. But it wouldn't have changed her lungs. Some things are in your hands. Some aren't."
Trisha thought. "Flashcards are in my hands."
"Exactly."

qa.q: What is Trisha going to make next time?
qa.a: Flashcards.

qa.q: What is Trisha worried about when she asks about Nani?
qa.a: She is worried and guilty, afraid that not visiting on Sunday made Nani sick.

qa.q: How did Ritu help Trisha?
qa.a: She praised the flashcard plan but clearly told her Nani's illness wasn't her fault, separating what is and isn't in her hands.

qa.q: What might Ritu be feeling when Trisha asks about Nani?
qa.a: Ritu is probably moved and concerned, wanting to lift a guilt her daughter shouldn't carry.

grounding: Illustrates a child who believes effort shapes results but starts blaming herself for an illness beyond her control.

passage: When our team lost the inter-school football match last year, 3-1, I went home and made a plan. I'm Pranav, and I've always thought that if I work at something, it gets better. So every morning before school I practised kicking against the garage wall, left foot, right foot. Eshaan came some days too. By March I scored in the practice match. That felt amazing. But then our coach moved to another city, and I thought it was my fault, as if I hadn't tried hard enough to make him want to stay. Eshaan said, "He got a new job, yaar. It's not about you." I think I believe him. Mostly.

qa.q: What was the score when the team lost?
What did Pranav feel when the coach moved away?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty and responsible, as if not trying hard enough had made the coach leave.

qa.q: How could Pranav keep the good part of this belief without the self-blame?
qa.a: Keep practising for things practice can change, and remember that other people's choices, like a new job, aren't Pranav's fault.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see the coach leaving?
qa.a: Eshaan sees it plainly as the coach getting a new job, nothing to do with Pranav.

grounding: Shows a child who believes effort shapes outcomes and practises after losing, but blames self for a coach leaving.

passage:
Coach's note, under-12 badminton, after the district tournament.
Tejas lost his second match 18–21. He shook hands, then went straight to the side court and practised backhand serves for twenty minutes. "If I practise, I'll get it," he told Santosh. That belief is his biggest strength.
But in his third match, the line judge called a clear in-shot out, and he lost the point. Afterwards he sat hunched on the bench. "I should have hit it further in. It's my fault." He looked miserable for the rest of the day.
What I did next: I told him his serve practice was exactly right. Then I explained that a line call is outside his control, and that it isn't his fault. We made two lists together: "Things I can change" and "Things I can't". The line call went in the second.

qa.q: What did Tejas practise after losing his second match?
qa.a: Backhand serves, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after the line call went against him?
qa.a: He felt guilty and miserable, blaming himself and saying, "It's my fault."

qa.q: How did the coach help Tejas keep his strength without self-blame?
qa.a: The coach praised his practice and made two lists with him, putting the line call under things he can't change.

qa.q: What might Santosh think when Tejas says practice will fix it?
qa.a: Santosh might feel inspired by Tejas's belief that effort matters, and may even want to practise with him.

grounding: Shows a coach noting a child who believes practice shapes results and tries again, but who blames himself for a call beyond his control.
